newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Religion enters British politics in election year.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Religion enters British politics in election year.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major prays in "all circumstances". Labour leader Tony Blair has a mission to restore Christian morality to socialism.

Religion, long regarded in Britain as an unsuitable bed fellow for politics, underpins the agenda ahead of the May 1 election as politicians trumpet their faith and the views of churchmen enjoy rare front-page billing.
Unlike the United States, where God is invoked on a daily basis, religion has rarely been a factor in British politics.
Previous leaders have been either agnostic, atheist, or members of the "weddings and funerals" brand of Anglicanism.

But the young leader of the opposition Labour Party has made religion fashionable with his proud Socialist Christian credentials and an evangelising zeal that has revamped his party after 18 years in the political cold.
Anxiety over a spate of violent crimes involving children, and the break-up of traditional family life have turned religion into a potential vote-winner for the first time in recent British politics.
Major has been persuaded to reveal his thoughts on religion to compete with Blair, whose profoundly held beliefs could give him the edge in the debate over society's moral decline.

"There is a recognition that society doesn't have much in the way of common values any more," said Jonathan Bartley, spokesman for the Movement for Christian Democracy, which promotes Judeo-Christian values in politics.

"There is a steady rise in crime, and however much the government increases the penalties it doesn't seem to do any good. People are looking for something different and searching desperately and religion is the obvious place to turn."
Blair, who talks with religious fervour of leading Britain into a new millennium, discovered his spiritual side while a student at Oxford University in the 1970s.
He attributes his conversion to Peter Thomson, an Australian Anglican priest 18 years his senior, who introduced him to the idea that one could act politically from a religious base.
BLAIR PUT RELIGION ON POLITICAL MAP

Blair, 43, put religion on the political map last year in an interview, scattered with references to Kant and Kierkegaard, which suggested that Conservative Party policies were incompatible with Christian teaching.
"Conservatives, I think, have too selfish a definition of self-interest. They fail to look beyond to the community and the individual's relationship with the community," Blair said.
His criticism of the Conservatives provoked howls of outrage and within weeks leading politicians of all parties were rushing to reveal the religious hearts on their sleeves.

A book spelling out the religious beliefs of party leaders was produced in late 1996. Major, displaying the faith of an ordinary Anglican church-goer, said his faith "adds life, reason and context to a set of rules."
"The Conservative Party is founded on principles flowing from the Christian faith," Major said, citing self-reliance, self-discipline and responsibility for one's actions.

Church leaders welcome the new interest in religious and moral values in a country which they fear has lost its soul, where people have become greedy and lost moral perspective in their drive for personal enrichment.
Cynics say the scent of sanctity is merely opportunism before an election.

"They seem to be seeing who can outpray the other. If I did believe in God I'd be praying to him to save us from sanctimonious politicians on their knees and claiming a hotline to heaven," remarked Labour MP Tony Banks.
WARY OF "FAMILY VALUES' AND ABORTION ISSUE

Politicians have been wary of trumpeting "family values" after Major's 1995 foray into this minefield blew up in his face with a string of revelations about Conservative MPs with secret illegitimate children, mistresses and dubious financial dealings.

Blair's religious background appeared to win support in October from the Roman Catholic Church which railed in a briefing against rampant capitalism and called for policies that emphasise social justice, fair wages and the common good.

Unusually, the Catholic document and its apparent endorsement of Labour made headline news. But the halo slipped when a Catholic archbishop attacked Blair's religious stance as a sham because of Labour's refusal to condemn abortion.
The Labour Party says abortion is a matter of conscience and allows MPs a free vote on the matter.

The abortion issue has yet to prove a major stumbling block for political converts to religion, and the Movement for Christian Democracy is wary of a "moral majority" of the kind seen in the United States.

"That is the big fear. No-one wants a new moral majority in this country. Christians need to be able to express their views across the whole range of issues and need to be happy about disagreeing with one another," said Bartley.
"To simply line up Christians behind the abortion issue only is a mistake and what a lot of Christians don't want," he said.
